blocks.text: But one thing seems to stand in the way of our fully accepting this rendering, and Fuller did not pass it over: namely, that none of the ancient Greeks observed the mournful and doleful wailings of the ostrich. Yet this (he says) we read not only reported of בת יענה bath jaana in Holy Scripture, but celebrated in striking words. Thus Mich. I, 8: “I will make a wailing like the dragons, and a mourning like the daughters of jaana.” And Iob. XXX, 28. 29: “I stood up in the congregation and cried out. I was a brother of dragons and a companion of the sons of jaana.” That is, even in the midst of an assembly of men I could not restrain myself from wailing with as strained a voice as the dragons and the daughters of jaana: the former take their name from mourning, the latter from crying out ^{(4)}. I reply: however diligently the Greek writers wrote on natural history, many things nevertheless escaped them even regarding the animals born in Greece. What wonder, then, if the same happens with unknown and foreign ones? Certainly, if this argument has any force, it will also follow from [col. 228] it that the ostrich is entirely ἄφωνον [aphōnon], since the Greeks wrote nothing whatever about its voice. Yet that it does have a voice is taught both by reason itself and by the records of the Arabs, to whom an Arabian bird ought to be better known than to the Greeks. [II, 825] In an Arabic book entitled الكفاية [al-Kifāya], as if one should say Sufficiency: يقال عار الظليم اذا صاح والزمار صياح الانثي [yuqāl ʿāra al-ẓalīm idhā ṣāḥa wa-l-zimār ṣiyāḥ al-unthā] The word arra is used of the male ostrich when it cries out, and zimar is the voice of the female. Hence Alcamus: عار الظليم صاح [ʿāra al-ẓalīm ṣāḥa] Arra, said of the male ostrich, that is, it cried out. And the cry itself is called عرار [ʿirār] irar; but زمرت النعام [zamarat al-naʿām] zamarath, that is, the female ostrich cried out. And elsewhere in the same Alcamus: رغا او رغي البعير والضبع والنعام صوت فصاح [raghā aw raghiya al-baʿīr wa-l-ḍabʿ wa-l-naʿām ṣawwata fa-ṣāḥa] Ragha or raghia, of the camel, the hyena and the ostrich: it cried out, it wailed. And again: رغا الصبي بكا اشد البكا [raghā al-ṣabī bakā ashadd al-bukā] Ragha, of a boy, that is, he wept bitterly. Moreover نقع [naqʿ] neke is the voice of the ostrich, and نقنق [naqnaqa] naknaka means the female ostrich clucked, when she laid eggs, or in flight and fear. Hence she herself is called نقنقة [niqniqa] niknika, and the male نقنق [niqniq] niknik. All this can be found in the Arabic lexicons. And lest you think these things rest on their testimony alone, here are the words of Johannes de Laet in his description of America, book 15, chapter 7: In the interior of Brazil many ostriches are found, which the natives call in their language janducocu, etc. They are tall, and cry so loudly that they are heard half a league away ^{(5)}. Indeed, I have more than once heard from those who lead ostriches about that the cry of ostriches is shrill and harsh, especially around dawn.
